newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU seen clearing Boeing /McDonnell deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU seen clearing Boeing /McDonnell deal.

text.p: The European Commission looked set on Wednesday to give its blessing in principle to a planned $15 billion plane manufacturing merger between Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp.
But a formal decision by the European Union's 20-seat executive, planned for today, was expected to be delayed for several days.
"I believe we will have a decision in principle...subject to verification of the details at a later stage," one EU source said.

Another said that concessions made by Boeing in an eleventh-hour bid to avert an EU block of the merger were "significant" and that the Commission was likely to approve the deal which will strengthen the group's position as the world's leading aeroplane maker.
"There will be no formal decision today, the aim is to approve it politically," a third source said, adding that the formal decision would be announced in several days.

Expectations of a deal, averting a potentially damaging transatlantic trade war between the EU and the United States, rose late on Tuesday after Boeing proposed scrapping exclusive supply pacts with three U.S. airlines.
The exclusive supply pacts with AMR Corp's American Airlines, Continental Airlines and Delta Air Lines had been one a key stumbling block in the talks.
Comments from EU Commissioners as they arrived for their weekly morning meeting in Brussels suggested that the internal debate could still be tough.
French commissioner Edith Cresson said she would resist clearing the deal despite the last-minute offer. "That doesn't change at all the heart of the problem," she told Reuters.

But her colleague Yves Thibault de Silguy, the commissioner for monetary affairs, was said by an EU source to have commented that Boeing's move was "a significant element to be taken into consideration".
"De Silguy will listen carefully to what (Competition Commissioner Karel) van Miert says about the sincerity and significance of Boeing's latest move," the source said.
Sweden's Anita Gradin, however, was more optimistic. "I'm sure," she said, when asked whether there would be a deal.
Van Miert was due to brief the EU's 20-seat executive and then announce the decision at a 1000 GMT news conference. Any decision will be based on a majority vote in the Commission.
Earlier French European Affairs Minister Pierre Moscovici said Boeing's late concessions did not go far enough and that the Commission would be firm with the U.S. plane giant.
"Boeing made concessions at the last minute. They do not seem complete to me," he told France Inter radio. "I think the Commission will be firm," he said, adding that Paris supported a tough stance.
In Bonn, German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said Europe must focus on strengthening the Airbus consortium in response to the planned U.S. merger rather than block the deal.

Kinkel told German radio that it might be necessary for European countries to provide public aid to Airbus to help the European aerospace group stay competitive in the face of new challenges from the United States.

"The point is that the Americans are leaving us behind in the aerospace industry and aerospace technology as a result of this merger and that we must make a decision regarding European industry policy and that can only mean that we strengthen Airbus," he said.
Kinkel indicated this could mean providing subsidies for the four-nation consortium owned by Daimler-Benz Aerospace, France's Aerospatiale, British Aerospace and Spain's Casa.
"...we must join together as Europeans and see that we remain competitive against the dominance of the American market in this area," he said.
